You report what others said with varied reporting verbs: assicurare, ammettere, negare, promettere, giurare, consigliare, raccomandare, vietare, avvertire, rimproverare, lamentarsi, insistere, with the right constructions and tenses.
nepitella (a Tuscan aromatic herb, similar to mint)

Graziella forbade him to write it down.
The doctor warned her that she mustn't tire herself out.

To use the verbs that take che + indicative: assicurare, ammettere, confessare, avvertire, giurare.
To use the verbs that take che + subjunctive: negare, insinuare (doubt), insistere perché.
To use the verbs that take di + infinitive: promettere, consigliare, suggerire, raccomandare, vietare, ordinare.
To use rimproverare qualcuno di and lamentarsi di / che.

To tell a story by reporting the words of several people.
Florence, end of June. After the neighbourhood festival, Graziella revealed to Karl the secret of the two per cent. The next day, Pietro tries to find out what she told him.
Well? What did Grandma tell you last night?
She made me swear not to tell anyone.
Not even me? I'm her grandson!
That's exactly what she said: "Not even Pietro." And she forbade me to write it in my notebook.
At least tell me whether it's an ingredient.

The fruit seller insinuates it's just salt.
Graziella warned me people would say all sorts. And she advised me not to answer.
And she didn't say anything to me?
Yes, she did. She asked me to tell you one thing: that you'll find out when you have a kitchen of your own.
But I don't want to be a cook!
I know. I told her. And she replied that everyone has a kitchen. Even journalists and teachers.
Il medico ha assicurato che stava bene.

Ha giurato che non lo sapeva.
These verbs present the information as fact, so they take the indicative. In the past, the sequence of tenses applies: "disse che stava bene / che sarebbe tornato".
Ha negato che ci fosse un segreto.
Ha insinuato che fosse solo sale.
Ha insistito perché restassi a cena.
Si lamentava che nessuno la ascoltasse.
"Negare che" almost always takes the subjunctive: "Nega che sia vero". The indicative ("nega che è vero") sounds colloquial.
Karl ha giurato di non dirlo.
Mi ha consigliato di non rispondere.
Mi ha raccomandato di dirti una cosa.
With these verbs, the imperative of direct speech becomes di + infinitive: "Non scriverlo!" → "Gli ha vietato di scriverlo."
L’ha rimproverato di aver messo l’aglio.

She reproaches him for his laziness.
She complains that she can't sleep.
After "rimproverare di" the infinitive is often compound, because the reproach is about something already done: "di aver detto", "di essere arrivato tardi".

The neighbourhood festival was held every year on the last Saturday in June, in piazza Santo Spirito, beneath the bare façade of Brunelleschi's church. There were craftsmen's stalls, the music school band, games for the children, and above all there was the dinner: long tables in the middle of the square, one for each street of the Oltrarno, and each street brought its own dish. For forty years, via Maggio's dish had been Graziella's ribollita. Three hundred portions, made in three enormous pots that the neighbourhood boys carried to the square on a cart, as if in procession. That year Dr Neri had been very clear: Graziella was not to cook for three hundred people, a month after her operation. He had forbidden it on the phone, then in person, then in writing, with a letter Marco had pinned up in the kitchen. Graziella had read it, folded it and said the doctor was right. Then she had added that Karl would make the ribollita. She would just watch.

Watching, for Graziella, meant sitting on a chair in the middle of the kitchen, with Guido's walking stick between her knees, and giving orders from five in the morning to six in the evening without ever getting up. Karl, Matei, Pietro and Bianca, who had asked to help "to learn on the job", worked for thirteen hours. They cut forty kilos of black cabbage, twenty of beans, fifteen of stale bread. Graziella checked everything. She reproached Matei for cutting the carrots too big. She warned Bianca that if she put the salt in before the beans, she'd send her home. She complained the heat was too high, then too low, then too high again. She insisted that Pietro taste each pot three times. And to Karl, at about four in the afternoon, when the three pots were ready, she said just one thing: "Tonight, after the festival, come to the kitchen. Alone." Karl asked why. Graziella didn't answer.

Bianca turned out to be a surprising helper. She had never cooked anything more complicated than a hard-boiled egg, but she listened with an attention Graziella appreciated at once. When the grandmother explained that the salt goes in only at the end, because beans salted early go hard, Bianca asked her why. Graziella looked at her in surprise: in fifty years no helper had ever asked her why. She explained. Bianca wrote it down in her notebook. Then she asked why the black cabbage is cut into strips and not squares, and why the bread has to be at least two days old. Graziella answered every question, one after another, and in the middle of the morning, when Bianca went to fetch water, she said quietly to Pietro: "This one asks the right questions. Like you. But she writes down the answers." Pietro protested that he wrote everything in the black notebook too. "You write the stories," replied Graziella. "She writes the recipes. A kitchen needs both."

The festival was the most beautiful the neighbourhood could remember. Perhaps because everyone knew about the operation, perhaps because it was the first summer after the flood that didn't happen in May, but there were more people in the square that evening than ever. The via Maggio table was the longest: there was the whole cooperative, Bellini, Efisio and Lucia, Rita, Guido, the fruit seller, Signor Franco, Valeria with her councillor's sash, Mancini with the cat Titolo in a basket, don Paolo come from San Leonardo with Signora Nunzia, and even Dr Ferraris, who now came to Florence so often that Graziella had started calling him "the via Maggio Milanese". When the three big pots arrived on the cart, pushed by Karl and Pietro, the square applauded. Graziella walked behind, leaning on Marco's arm, with her slow but determined step. She sat down at the head of the table, had a bowl brought to her and tasted. The whole table held its breath. Graziella nodded. "Ninety-eight," she said. The square applauded again.

After dinner the music school band struck up a waltz, and the square turned into a ballroom. Guido asked the fruit seller to dance; she refused twice and then danced for an hour. Efisio and Lucia danced as at their wedding, in 1968, slowly and precisely, while everyone stopped to watch. Dr Ferraris asked Signora Nunzia, who was ninety-two and had a stick, and she accepted on condition she could dance sitting down: so Ferraris danced standing in front of her chair, holding her hands, and the square applauded. Viola danced with Lupino, holding him by his front paws, until the dog got tired and lay down under the table. Pietro, after a long hesitation and a nudge from Davide, asked Bianca. She said yes. They danced badly, treading on each other's feet, laughing. Graziella watched them from the head of the table, sitting next to Bellini. "Do you remember our first dance?" Bellini asked her. "At Giulia's wedding, in Sorrento." "I remember you trod on my feet," replied Graziella. "Like those two."

Around midnight, when the festival was over and the square was emptying, Karl went back to the trattoria. The lights were off, except in the kitchen. Graziella was sitting at the wooden table, glasses on her nose and, in front of her, the unlabelled glass jar she had taken to hospital and brought back home without ever opening it. Next to the jar was a small terracotta pot, old and chipped, with a plant with small greyish leaves. Karl recognised it: it was the pot that had always stood on the kitchen window sill, the one nobody was ever allowed to touch. Graziella gestured to him to sit down. Then, without saying anything, she opened the jar and handed it to him. Karl sniffed. It was a scent he knew, because he had smelled it every morning in the kitchen for three months without being able to name it: fresh, slightly bitter, between mint and oregano. "Nepitella," said Graziella. "Dried. From that plant there."

Karl asked why only two per cent. Why not more, if it was so good. Graziella smiled the way you smile at a child asking why the sky is blue. "If you put in more," she said, "it covers everything. You taste only that, and the ribollita becomes something else. If you put in less, you can't taste anything." She paused, turning the jar over in her hands. "It's like nostalgia," she said. "A pinch makes you want to go home. Too much ruins your day." Karl thought about it for a long time. He thought of his mother in Marsaxlokk, the harbour with the colourful boats, the smell of fried fish on Sundays. A pinch of nostalgia. He understood that Graziella's ribollita, for fifty-four years, had had in it a pinch of Bologna, a pinch of Aldo, a pinch of a man who came on foot through the mud and brought his mother's garden with him. "So it isn't an ingredient," he said quietly. "It's a person." Graziella didn't answer. But her eyes were moist.

Then she told him the story. She told it slowly, in a low voice, the way you tell something you have never told anyone. Aldo had brought the plant in 1975, on the day of the wedding. It was a cutting taken from his mother's garden, in Bologna, in a yoghurt pot. Aldo had put it on the kitchen window sill and said that this trattoria lacked only one thing: a bit of his home. Graziella had laughed. Then, one evening, by chance, she had put a few nepitella leaves in the ribollita. Her father, who had never changed a comma of his mother's recipe, tasted it, was silent for a long time and then said: "This is better." Since then, for fifty-four years, every pot of ribollita had had a pinch of nepitella from that plant. When the plant got old, Graziella took a cutting and replanted it in the same pot. It was the same plant of Aldo's. For fifty-four years.

Karl was silent for a long time, the jar in his hand. Then he asked, quietly, why she was telling him. Graziella took off her glasses and cleaned them with her apron. "Because you learned the ninety-eight per cent without asking for the two," she said. "And because in May, when I was in hospital, you kept my trattoria open. Whoever keeps a trattoria open has the right to know what's inside it." Then she made him swear three things. The first: not to tell anyone, "not even Pietro". The second: never to write it in his notebook, "because written things get read by someone sooner or later". The third: to take a cutting from the plant every year, "so that when I'm gone, Aldo's plant will stay in this kitchen". Karl swore all three, with his hand on his heart, as his mother had taught him in Malta. Graziella nodded. Then she closed the jar again and gave it to him. "It's yours," she said. "Not the pot. The pot stays on the window sill."

Karl walked home that night, along deserted via Maggio, the jar in his pocket and his hand closed over it, as if someone might steal it. The street lamps made the stones shine. He passed Guido's shoemaker's, the 1966 plaque, the trattoria's brass plaque. He thought of Aldo, whom he had never known, and who in 1975 had walked that same street with a yoghurt pot in his hand. When he got to his room, he couldn't sleep. At two he phoned his mother, in Malta, who answered worried, convinced something had happened. Karl told her everything was fine, that he just wanted to hear her voice. His mother understood there was something, but asked no questions. She talked about the harbour, the boats, the neighbour who had bought a dog. Karl listened, with the jar on his bedside table. He told her nothing about the secret. But before hanging up he asked her whether his grandmother's mint was still in the garden at home. His mother said yes. Karl smiled in the dark.

The next morning, at six, when Pietro came down to the kitchen, he found Karl already at the stove, with a strange expression, half happy and half frightened, like someone carrying a precious burden. Pietro understood at once. "She told you," he said. Karl didn't answer. Pietro asked him what his grandmother had told him. Karl replied that she had made him swear not to tell anyone. Pietro protested that he was her grandson. Karl replied that Graziella had said exactly that: "Not even Pietro." And that she had even forbidden him to write it in his notebook. Pietro insisted for a quarter of an hour, with all the argumentation techniques he had learned at the tournament, the competition, Researchers' Night. Karl resisted them all. In the end Pietro asked for at least a clue. Karl thought about it. "I can tell you she admitted there's an ingredient," he said. "And that she denied it's a spice." Pietro wrote it in the black notebook. It was all he had.

Pietro asked Bianca for help. That very evening, on the trattoria steps, he told her everything he knew: an ingredient, not a spice, and the fact, which Karl had let slip, that the recipe had changed once, many years ago. Bianca listened with a frown, as if in front of a maths problem. Then she said they had to proceed by hypotheses, as the cooperative had done with the Madonna of San Leonardo. If it wasn't a spice, it was a herb, a cheese or a kind of bread. If it had changed once, there had to be a date. And if there was a date, perhaps there was a trace. Pietro remembered his grandmother's squared notebook, the accounts book from 1974. They looked for it together the next morning, in the pantry. They leafed through 1975 page by page. In mid-September, next to the wedding accounts, they found a line in Graziella's young handwriting: "Little pot. Gift from A. To keep on the window sill." Bianca looked at Pietro. Pietro looked at the window. Neither of them said anything.

By midday the news had gone round the neighbourhood. Nobody knew how. Karl swore he hadn't said anything. Pietro swore he hadn't said anything. But by eleven the fruit seller already knew that "Graziella had revealed the secret to the Maltese", and by midday the baker, the bar, the newsstand and the shoemaker's knew it too. From that moment began what Mancini later called "the great ribollita mystery". Everyone had a theory. The fruit seller insinuated that it was just salt, "because Graziella always salts at the end, I've seen her". The baker maintained that it was the bread, a special bread he made for her himself on Thursdays, even though Graziella had always denied buying different bread from everyone else. Guido was convinced it was red wine. Efisio said it was Sardinian pecorino, "because all good things come from Sardinia". Signor Franco, ninety, said only that the secret was patience, and that you couldn't buy that at the market.

On Thursday the fruit seller tried a direct assault. When Karl came by the market to buy black cabbage, she kept him at her stall for a quarter of an hour, offering him first a discount, then a crate of peaches for free, then the promise of introducing him to her niece, who was "pretty, capable and without a boyfriend". In return she wanted just one word. Karl, who had learned the right formulas at the via Maggio school of letters, answered with the most formal politeness he could muster. He told her he thanked her most sincerely for the interest shown, that he greatly appreciated the offer of the peaches and that of the niece, but that he found himself obliged, much to his regret, to decline both. The fruit seller looked at him open-mouthed. Then she burst out laughing so loudly that her customers turned round. "This one talks like a notary," she told the whole market. "Graziella chose well. You'll get nothing out of him." And she gave him the peaches anyway. For free.

On Tuesday Mancini decided to carry out an investigation. It was, he said, the first real scoop of his career since he had discovered the Matteo Popov mistake. He went to the trattoria with his notebook and interviewed everyone, one by one, with the seriousness of an investigative journalist. He asked Graziella whether it was true that there was a secret. Graziella denied that there was any secret. She said the ribollita was the same as her grandmother's, and that anyone who said otherwise was a gossip. Then he asked Karl whether Graziella had revealed anything to him. Karl admitted she had talked to him, but refused to say what about, invoking, he said, "professional secrecy". Mancini reminded him he was neither a doctor nor a lawyer. Karl replied that he was a restorer, and that restorers, like doctors, never reveal what's under the paint without the owner's permission. Mancini wrote the answer down word for word. He liked it so much he used it as his headline.

The article came out the following Sunday, on the culture page, with the headline: "The restorer who won't reveal what's under the ribollita". Mancini told the whole story in the tone of a detective novel. He reported that Signora Graziella had categorically denied that a secret existed, but had admitted, "under pressure", that the recipe had changed once, in 1975. He reported that the Maltese intern had sworn to reveal nothing, invoking the professional secrecy of restorers. He reported the neighbourhood's theories, one by one, with the name of whoever held them. And he concluded with a sentence that made Graziella furious for three days: "The journalist takes the liberty of suggesting that readers look carefully at the kitchen window sill. He doesn't say why. But a good journalist, like a good restorer, knows how to look where others don't." On Monday morning, in front of the kitchen window, on the pavement, there were seven people looking at the pot.

Within a week Graziella's pot had become a tourist attraction. Someone photographed the window sill and put the photo online with the caption: "The secret of Florence's most famous ribollita?". The photo went round everyone's phones. Tourists began stopping in front of the kitchen window to photograph the plant, sometimes taking a selfie next to it. An American food blogger came specially from Rome, asked to interview Graziella and was greeted with a sentence Davide swore he heard with his own ears: "Young lady, that's a plant. Plants don't give interviews." A group of Japanese students left a thank-you note on the window sill, written in perfect Italian, for "the plant that makes the ribollita good". Graziella, who saw everything from the kitchen, grew redder every day. Mancini, when he came for dinner, was met with such an icy silence that he preferred to eat standing up, at the counter, without taking off his jacket.

Graziella moved the pot that very morning, before eight, from the window sill to a kitchen cupboard, in the dark, where the plant immediately began to suffer. Karl reproached her for putting it in the dark. Graziella reproached him for talking to Mancini. Karl swore he hadn't said anything about the pot. Graziella insinuated that Mancini had an informant. For two days there was a heavy silence in the kitchen, broken only by "pass me the salt" and "turn that heat off". On the third day the plant's leaves were yellow. Karl, without asking permission, put it back on the window sill. Graziella saw, opened her mouth to say something, then closed it. She looked at the plant breathing again in the light. "You did the right thing," she said at last, quietly. "Plants aren't to be hidden. Nor are secrets, in the end. You just protect them." Then she added that if anyone touched that pot, she would chase them with the ladle all the way to Porta Romana. Karl wrote it on a sign and hung it in the window.

It was Viola who solved the mystery, without meaning to. One evening, while Giulia was putting her to bed, she asked her whether she knew what was in Granny Graziella's ribollita. Giulia said no. Viola seemed very surprised. "I know," she said. "It's Grandpa Aldo's plant. The one on the window. Granny Graziella makes me smell it when I'm sad." Giulia was speechless. The next day, very delicately, she told Graziella. Graziella didn't get angry. She laughed, instead, so hard that she had to sit down. "Fifty-four years," she said when she could speak, "fifty-four years I've kept it secret, and a six-year-old knows." Then she explained that yes, it was true: when Viola was sad, she took her to the window and made her smell the leaves, because they had always done her good. She had never thought a little girl could understand. "I told her it was Grandpa Aldo's plant," she said. "I didn't tell her it went in the pot. She worked it out herself. She's a born restorer."

The next day Graziella called Viola into the kitchen and had her climb onto a stool, in front of the window. She taught her to recognise herbs by their scent, one at a time, with her eyes closed: basil, rosemary, sage, bay, and last of all the nepitella from Aldo's plant. Viola recognised them all at the first try, except the bay, which she confused with rosemary. Graziella told her she was very good, better than Karl, who had taken three weeks. Then she gave her an official job, written on a sheet in red marker, which Viola pinned above her bed: "Viola Popa Esposito, keeper of the pot." The keeper had three duties: to water the plant on Mondays and Thursdays, to make sure no tourist touched it, and to say nothing to anyone. Viola took on the job with enormous seriousness. All summer, on Mondays and Thursdays, she climbed onto the stool with a glass of water and watered Aldo's plant, counting the drops out loud.

That evening Graziella did something nobody expected. She called Pietro, Karl, Giulia and Viola into the kitchen, closed the door and said that, since by now everyone knew except the neighbourhood, she might as well tell it properly. She told the story of 1975 again, of Aldo and the yoghurt pot, of her father who had said "this is better". Pietro listened in silence, the black notebook on his knees but his pen still. When Graziella finished, he asked whether he could write it down. Graziella thought for a long time. Then she said no. She explained that some stories shouldn't be written, but told, aloud, from one person to another, in a kitchen. "If you write it," she said, "it becomes a recipe. If you tell it, it stays a story." Then she made him promise that one day he would tell it in his turn, to someone who would have a kitchen. "But I don't want to be a cook," Pietro protested. Graziella smiled. "Everyone has a kitchen," she said. "Even journalists and teachers."

For the neighbourhood, the mystery remained a mystery. Graziella forbade everyone to confirm any theory. When the fruit seller asked her for the umpteenth time whether it was salt, Graziella told her that yes, it was salt, and that she bought it from her. The fruit seller, who didn't sell salt, was confused for a week. To the baker she said it was his bread, and the baker was so happy he gave her a loaf a day for a month. To Guido she said it was wine, to Efisio pecorino. To Mancini, when he came back with his notebook, she said that the secret was that there was no secret, and that journalists should deal with serious matters. Mancini published that statement too, with the headline: "Signora Graziella denies the existence of the secret. The window sill declines to comment." Everyone in the neighbourhood remained convinced they were right. And everyone, when they ate the ribollita, tasted their own secret. "That's how it works," Graziella told Karl. "Everyone puts in what they want to find."

The last attempt was made by Dr Ferraris, in his own way. One evening, after dinner, he asked Graziella for a word in private. He told her that the group he worked for had two hundred company canteens all over Italy, and would be prepared to pay a substantial sum for the ribollita recipe, with her name on the packaging. Graziella listened to the end, arms folded. Then she asked him how much. Ferraris named a figure. Graziella didn't bat an eyelid. "Not the price," she said. "The conditions." Ferraris smiled, recognising the phrase. He asked what the conditions were. "Just one," replied Graziella. "You come yourself, in person, to this kitchen, at five in the morning, for three months. Learn to make it. Then you teach it to your cooks yourself, one by one. Without a notebook." Ferraris was silent for a long time. Then he laughed, raised his hands and said he surrendered. "I knew you'd say that," he admitted. "I just wanted to hear you say it."

At the end of the summer Karl took the first cutting from Aldo's plant, as he had sworn. He put it in a yoghurt pot, as Aldo had done in 1975, and took it to his room with the window onto the courtyard. The cutting took root in two weeks. When he told Graziella, she didn't answer at once. Then she asked him whether he had ever thought of going back to Malta, one day, to open a trattoria. Karl said no: he was a restorer, not a cook. Graziella nodded. "I know," she said. "But if one day you have a kitchen, in Malta or wherever you like, take the plant with you. That way Aldo will have gone all round the Mediterranean." Karl promised. Then he asked, with some hesitation, whether he could at least tell his mother that the ribollita had a secret. Graziella thought about it. "You can tell her it has one," she said. "You can't tell her what it is. And tell her that if she comes to Florence, I'll make her the ribollita myself. With the two per cent."

That evening Pietro opened the black notebook and wrote the date. Then he sat for a long time with his pen hovering over the page. He had promised his grandmother not to write the story of the plant, and he always kept his promises. So he wrote something else, a whole page of reported speech, as his Italian teacher had taught him. "Grandma said some stories shouldn't be written. She made me promise to tell it one day to someone who will have a kitchen. Karl swore not to tell anyone. The fruit seller insinuated it was salt, the baker maintained it was bread, Mancini suggested looking at the window sill. Grandma denied everything, then admitted everything, then told everyone they were right." He reread the page. Then he added a line, the last: "Viola said she had always known. She's the only one who didn't swear anything." And he smiled, because that, at least, was a sentence his grandmother hadn't forbidden him to write.
